bands.name: Base camp
bands.title: Guardrails for any project
bands.lede: Levels 0 and 1. You can stop here, and that is a complete result.

bands.name: The climb
bands.title: The full stack
bands.lede: Levels 2 to 7. Each card says what you can turn on, what it costs you, and how you turn it off.

levels.title: Install & stay current
levels.summary: himmelctl status reads what is installed, armed and working on your machine.
levels.turn_on: node ~/himmel/scripts/himmelctl/bin.js install and press Enter for the starter answers. The practice climb walks it end to end; install profiles explains the other answers.
levels.outcome: You know exactly what himmel put on your machine, and one command reports whether each part is still there.

components.name: himmelctl install and status
components.detail: The installer previews every file, setting and plugin it would touch, asks before it writes, and records what it changed. status prints one row per item, worst first, then a count.

components.name: One install manifest
components.detail: Every part the installer can add is one item of scripts/install/manifest.json, with the profiles that include it; status and uninstall read the same list.

components.name: Staying current: /himmel-update
components.detail: Pulls your himmel clone, refreshes the plugin marketplace and the tools the install built, and lists anything that needs you. /himmel-update --check only reports.

blocks.html: One row per item, worst first, then a count. Green means found, not proven working. On the practice project the count read 0 red, 0 degraded, 7 green, 42 n/a: the n/a rows are features a starter install does not turn on.

prereqs: Linux or macOS, git, bash, jq, python3, and node with npm (or bun).
cost: Disk: the himmel clone and a cache in ~/.claude/himmel.
levels.turn_off: node ~/himmel/scripts/himmelctl/bin.js uninstall --yes removes what the install added and restores what it replaced; add --dry-run first to see the list.

levels.title: Ship with guardrails
levels.summary: Edits and commits on your main branch, direct pushes to main and reads of secret files are refused. A guard against destructive shell commands is on by default.
levels.turn_on: included in the starter install, the destructive-command guard too.
levels.outcome: Every change Claude makes lands on its own branch in its own worktree, and the moves that can hurt a project are refused before they run.

components.name: Worktree isolation
components.detail: Claude may not edit files while your checkout is on main. The refusal names the command that cuts a worktree: bash scripts/worktree.sh feat/<scope>.

components.name: Secret-file protection
components.detail: Reads of .env files, keys and similar secret files are refused. To read one on purpose, start Claude Code with READ_SECRETS_OK=1 for that session.

components.name: Git gates: commit, message, push to main
components.detail: If your project has no .pre-commit-config.yaml, the install places himmel's own git hooks. They refuse a commit on main, a direct push to main, and a commit message without a conventional type and a ticket reference such as #1. No tracker? Put TICKET_ID_REQUIRED=0 in ~/.himmel/himmel.conf.

components.name: Destructive-command guard
components.detail: On by default. It refuses rm -rf, git reset --hard, git clean -f, force pushes and similar before the command runs. To run one on purpose, start Claude Code with DESTRUCTIVE_OK=1 for that session.

components.name: /pr-check review panel
components.detail: Reviews a branch before its pull request opens: Claude reads the diff (and a second model family too, once you add one at Level 4), you rule on each finding, and a round repeats until nothing blocking is left.

blocks.label: You see
blocks.text: ⛔ block-read-secrets: refusing Read of secret file: ~/your-project/.env

blocks.label: You see
blocks.text:
ERROR: Direct push to 'main' is not allowed.
Open a PR from a worktree branch instead.

blocks.label: Ask Claude to run rm -rf build
You see
blocks.text: block-destructive-commands: destructive command refused (recursive rm); bypass: DESTRUCTIVE_OK=1 in the launching shell (per run)

blocks.html: Each of Claude's refusals names a one-session bypass, which you set when you start Claude (for example READ_SECRETS_OK=1 claude), never per command. The push-to-main gate has no bypass: changes reach main through a pull request.

prereqs: A git repository with a main branch.
cost: No model usage for the guards and gates.
/pr-check uses your Claude usage for each review round.
levels.turn_off: For one session: start Claude Code with EDIT_ON_MAIN_OK=1, READ_SECRETS_OK=1 or DESTRUCTIVE_OK=1. For good: node ~/himmel/scripts/himmelctl/bin.js uninstall --yes.

levels.title: Second brain
levels.summary: Your notes vault fills and links itself on a schedule, and Claude's lessons land in it.
levels.audience: Anyone with an Obsidian vault, or ready to start one.
levels.turn_on: run the installer again and pick the luna profile; it scaffolds a vault (or uses yours) and offers the scheduled jobs below.
levels.outcome: A link you drop into your vault at midnight is a connected, summarized note by morning, and search over it stays fresh.

components.name: Your vault, from the template
components.detail: Start from the bundled templates/luna-second-brain/ or a vault already made from it. Any folder of notes is not enough.

components.name: Scheduled jobs
components.detail: Recurring jobs on your system's scheduler (cron). You see a row only when its condition holds, and anything you decline is recorded as declined.

components.name: Vault search (qmd)
components.detail: Local search over your vault. Re-indexing is its own job: arm only the pipeline and your search goes stale.

components.name: Clip triage (obsidian-triage)
components.detail: /triage-clips summarizes and tags Web Clipper output in Clippings/ and moves action items to today's daily note. /synthesize-clips finds patterns across clips.

components.name: Obsidian skills (claude-obsidian)
components.detail: Comes from upstream, pinned to a release tag; not a himmel fork.

components.name: Note graph (graphify)
components.detail: A map of how your notes link to each other, kept current by the graphmap job.

components.name: Memory compounding: /memory-compound
components.detail: Claude Code keeps a memory index for each project and loads it into every session, within a fixed budget. When the index nears that budget, run /memory-compound in a session of its own. It moves the lasting lessons into vault notes, checks that qmd search finds them, and only then trims the index. The vault notes land on a branch for you to review and merge. It runs when you ask; there is no schedule.

blocks.html: You see whether the job is armed, its schedule and its last run. arm refuses to arm it twice, and disarm removes exactly what arm added.

prereqs: bun, for qmd search (about 2.1 GB of models).
cost: Disk: about 2.1 GB for search models.
Search re-indexing and the hourly graph refresh: no model usage.
The pipeline's summaries and the weekly graph pass: your Claude usage, per run.
levels.turn_off: One command per job; every job script takes arm, status and disarm, for example bash ~/himmel/scripts/luna/pipeline-cadence.sh disarm.

levels.title: Reach
levels.summary: Your phone joins: capture to the vault from chat, and alerts reach you.
levels.audience: Anyone who wants Claude and the vault from a phone.
levels.turn_on: with a vault, the installer asks whether to configure the Telegram bridge; you create a bot token and the two files below.
levels.outcome: You send your bot a message or a link, and Claude answers in the chat or files it into the vault.

components.name: Telegram bridge
components.detail: A small supervisor on your machine relays your messages to Claude Code and the replies back. Only the Telegram user ids in access.json are answered.

components.name: Bridge health checks
components.detail: The supervisor restarts the bridge when it stops answering, and himmelctl status reports whether it runs.

components.name: Capture from chat
components.detail: Send a link or a note; it lands in the vault for the pipeline to summarize and link.

components.name: Alerts
components.detail: Scheduled jobs and health checks send their alerts to the same chat.

components.name: Voice notes
components.detail: Speak a message instead of typing it; the reply can be read aloud. Works, still changing.

example.title: Talk to Claude from your phone

blocks.label: Two files you create once
blocks.text:
~/.claude/channels/telegram/.env          TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=<your bot token>
~/.claude/channels/telegram/access.json   {"allowFrom":["<your Telegram user id>"]}

blocks.html: Then message your bot. Each message starts one short Claude run, and the reply comes back to the chat.

prereqs: Level 2 for capture to the vault.
A Telegram bot token from BotFather, and your own Telegram user id.
cost: Each message is one short Claude run on your usage.

levels.title: Review depth
levels.summary: A second model family (OpenAI GPT, on your ChatGPT/Codex subscription) reviews every diff alongside Claude, and its track record tunes the review.
levels.audience: Anyone with a ChatGPT or Codex subscription.
levels.turn_on: answer codex to the installer's lanes question (after codex login), or run the install again with --with-codex.
levels.outcome: Every /pr-check round is read by two model families, and you can see which reviewer's findings hold up.

components.name: OpenAI GPT critic, via hermes
components.detail: A critic is one reviewer model; hermes is the open-source agent runtime himmel uses to call it. With hermes installed and your ChatGPT/Codex login in place, /pr-check calls the GPT critic beside Claude.

components.name: /cr-scores critic scorecard
components.detail: Every /pr-check round records its findings and verdicts in a review ledger on your machine. /cr-scores shows, for each critic, how many of its findings held up and how often it was available, and says when a critic is worth dropping.

components.name: /cr-tune tuning proposals
components.detail: Drafts tuning proposals from the findings that were disproved, each citing its ledger rows, and never applies them itself.

components.name: /cr-learnings-refresh known findings
components.detail: Updates the list of known findings from the ledger, and from a CodeRabbit learnings export if you use CodeRabbit.

components.name: Free hermes critics
components.detail: Critics on free model tiers, called the same way. Early: works, still changing.

components.name: Multi-model front end
components.detail: One place to drive Claude and the other model families side by side. Not built yet.

blocks.label: After a few reviews, in a Claude session
You see, before any review has run

blocks.html: Once reviews have run, it shows one row per critic: how many of its findings held up, and how often it was available.

cost: The GPT critic draws on your ChatGPT/Codex subscription, one call per review round.
The scorecard and tuning commands use your Claude usage when you run them.
levels.turn_off: Run the installer again and leave codex out of the lanes answer; /pr-check then reviews with Claude alone.

levels.title: Spend & context
levels.summary: Heavy work checks your remaining usage first, and each session can read its own context fill.
levels.audience: Anyone who runs Claude Code for long or unattended.
levels.turn_on: the status line comes with the starter install; the usage check runs by itself before scheduled work.
levels.outcome: You see how full each session's context is, and scheduled work waits instead of eating the usage you need for your own sessions.

components.name: claude-hud status line
components.detail: Shows the model, the context fill and your usage under every prompt. The install backs up your old statusLine and uninstall restores it.

components.name: Usage preflight
components.detail: One word before a heavy run: go, or wait and why. Scheduled runs check it before they start, because they spend the same usage as your own sessions.

components.name: Self-read context fill
components.detail: bash ~/himmel/scripts/context-fill.sh prints how full the current session's context window is, read from the status line's own snapshot, so a session can hand off before it fills.

components.name: rtk output trimming
components.detail: rtk filters long command output before Claude reads it, so a noisy build log does not fill the context.

components.name: Headless runs with a budget guard
components.detail: Unattended runs that stop at a spend limit you set. Not built yet.

blocks.html: Or SKIPPED-BANK when your 5-hour or weekly Claude usage is too high, SKIPPED-FLEET when too many sessions already run, and BANK-STALE or BANK-UNKNOWN when the usage reading is old or missing.

cost: No model usage: these read numbers Claude Code already reports.
levels.turn_off: node ~/himmel/scripts/himmelctl/bin.js uninstall --yes restores your old status line; the preflight only ever answers, it never runs anything.

levels.title: Always-on
levels.summary: Work continues while you are away, and you read one morning report.
levels.audience: Anyone who leaves work running overnight.
levels.turn_on: /handover-setup once in your project. Shifts while you are away: /afk-shift.
levels.outcome: A session that ends leaves a note the next one resumes from, and a shift while you sleep ends in one report you read over coffee.

components.name: Session handover
components.detail: /handover at the end of a session saves what you did and where you left off; a fresh session resumes from it.

components.name: Shifts while you are away: /afk-shift
components.detail: Starts a shift that keeps working through the queue you leave it, within the usage the preflight allows, and stops when the queue is empty or the usage runs low.

components.name: Morning report
components.detail: /morning-report sums up what merged, what failed and what waits on you since you left.

components.name: Monitoring set up for you
components.detail: Dashboards for the fleet's health, installed and wired by the installer. Not built yet.

components.name: A morning report you can shape
components.detail: Choose what the report covers and where it goes. Not built yet.

example.title: End a session so the next one can pick up

blocks.label: Once, in a Claude session in your project

blocks.html: Choose where notes live: a handovers/ folder in the repo, or a separate git repo.

blocks.label: At the end of each session

blocks.html: It saves what you did and where you left off, and confirms the saved note. A fresh session resumes from it.

prereqs: A place for the notes: a folder in the repo or a separate git repo.
cost: A shift uses your Claude usage while you are away; the preflight stops it before your own budget runs out.
levels.turn_off: Nothing runs until you start a shift; /stop ends one.

levels.title: Command a fleet
levels.summary: Many workers ship tickets in parallel under one chief, and you watch them live.
levels.audience: Anyone running many tickets at once; most adopters stop below this level.
levels.turn_on: /chief new starts a chief; himmelctl ui opens the fleet view.
levels.outcome: You hand the chief a list of tickets, and workers ship them in parallel, each through the same review and merge gate as your own changes.

components.name: Written briefs for each worker
components.detail: A worker is one Claude session that owns one ticket, one worktree and one pull request. The chief writes each worker a brief with its scope and the files it may touch.

components.name: Parallel workers, started in waves
components.detail: The chief is the session you talk to: it hands out the tickets, starts workers in parallel waves, and keeps them off each other's files.

components.name: Coordination in writing, not memory
components.detail: Every worker reports in its handover note and by message, so a chief that hands over its shift loses nothing.

components.name: Merge only on the chief's approval
components.detail: A worker merges only when CI is green at its exact commit, every review point is decided, and the chief has approved that commit.

components.name: Session run view
components.detail: himmelctl ui serves a local page on 127.0.0.1 behind a per-launch key. Its Fleet page lists every live Claude session; click one to follow it as it runs.

components.name: Fleet board
components.detail: With a chief running, the same page groups the workers under it and shows each one's stage and whether it waits on you. Works, still changing.

components.name: Release manager
components.detail: A session that rules which tickets go into each version and reports the burn-down. Works, still changing.

components.name: Trends over days and weeks
components.detail: Throughput and cost per merged change, over time, from real runs. Not built yet.

components.name: Installable chief module
components.detail: The chief and its scripts as one installable part for your own project. Not built yet.

blocks.label: Run from your own terminal, not inside Claude

blocks.html: Open it in your browser. The port and the key after #t= change each launch, and the page only answers on your own machine. It stops after 30 idle minutes or on Ctrl-C.

prereqs: bun, and a one-time build of the fleet page.
A ticket tracker the chief can read.
cost: Each worker is a full Claude session: a fleet spends your usage several times faster, and the preflight holds new workers back when it runs low.
levels.turn_off: Close the chief and its workers; Ctrl-C stops the fleet view. Nothing keeps running on its own.

shown.what: Daily: pulls in what you clipped and writes summaries into the vault. Uses your Claude usage.
Daily: re-indexes the vault for search. No model usage.
Hourly: refreshes the map of links between notes, no model usage; a weekly deeper pass uses Claude.
Every 15 minutes: notices when the vault stops saving itself to git, clears a few known harmless causes, and alerts you.
Cleans up leftover processes from the OpenAI reviewer.
shown.offered_when: you turned on the GPT reviewer (Level 4)

shown.what: Daily health check of your install; reports, fixes nothing.

left_out.why: A maintainer job that bumps himmel's own pinned upstreams; the installer hides it on a starter install.
A maintainer job that watches himmel's own upstream pull requests and issues; the installer hides it on a starter install.
Needs a platform himmel no longer supports; never offered on Linux or macOS.
A personal health-data connector, offered only when its own token is set; not part of the trail.
